strengths: Comprehensive and diverse domain coverage across eight classic and challenging combinatorial optimization problems (routing, scheduling, location, graph, and tree problems).

Pushes evaluation scale by orders of magnitude compared to prior ML4CO benchmarks (e.g., TSP up to 10M nodes, MIS up to 8M nodes), directly addressing the synthetic/toy-scale limitation pervasive in the literature.

Rigorous, unified cross-paradigm evaluation encompassing 16 ML methods (end-to-end neural solvers, neural-enhanced heuristics, and LLM-based agentic code generation) against industry-grade and competition-winning classical solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX, KaMIS, LKH-3, HGS, SCIP-Jack).

Provides valuable empirical insights and diagnostic analyses, including ablations on the utility of neural guidance, investigation into the failure of GNNs on non-Euclidean/global structure (STP/ATSP), and analysis of algorithms synthesized by LLM agents.
weaknesses: Distribution shift vs. solver capability: The neural models are evaluated on hard, large-scale competition instances while being trained on smaller synthetic distributions (e.g., RB models or unit square TSP). While realistic for zero-shot generalization testing, it remains somewhat decoupled from whether neural methods could perform better if trained directly on domain-specific or multi-scale data.

Hardware parity across solver paradigms: Classical solvers and LLM-generated code are evaluated on a single CPU core, whereas neural solvers utilize an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU in addition to CPU cores, making direct wall-clock time comparisons somewhat hardware-dependent.

strengths: Comprehensive and timely benchmark: FRONTIERCO spans eight distinct combinatorial optimization problem classes (MIS, MDS, TSP, CVRP, CFLP, CPMP, FJSP, STP), providing much broader coverage than existing routing- or graph-only benchmarks.

Realistic scale and structural complexity: By incorporating competition-grade instances and scaling up to millions of nodes (e.g., TSP up to 10M cities, MIS up to 8M nodes), the benchmark directly addresses the pervasive limitation of toy/synthetic evaluations in the ML4CO literature.

Broad cross-paradigm comparison: Evaluates 16 representative ML solvers—encompassing end-to-end neural methods, neural-guided heuristics, and LLM-based program synthesis agents—against dedicated state-of-the-art classical solvers (e.g., KaMIS, LKH-3, HGS, SCIP-Jack, Gurobi, CPLEX).

Valuable empirical insights: The study provides rigorous evidence regarding the limitations of current neural solvers under distribution shifts, out-of-memory bottlenecks, and non-Euclidean/global structures (e.g., Section 5.2), while critically analyzing the metaheuristic strategies discovered by LLM agents.
weaknesses: Asymmetry in computational budget and fairness: While all test evaluations are capped at one hour, LLM agents undergo an offline search/evolutionary phase (64 iterations with 300s validation timeouts using o4-mini) and neural solvers use an RTX A6000 GPU, whereas classical baselines are run on a single CPU core without problem-specific hyperparameter re-tuning.

Impact of failure penalty on aggregate metrics: Assigning a primal gap of 1.0 (100%) to any out-of-memory or infeasible run heavily penalizes solvers in the arithmetic mean gap. Reporting the feasibility/completion rate explicitly alongside the gap conditional on feasibility would provide a clearer breakdown of solver performance.

Under-explored retraining on realistic distributions: The paper highlights that neural models suffer under severe distribution shift because they were trained on uniform/synthetic generators. It remains partially unclear whether this gap is fundamentally architectural or primarily a data distribution limitation that could be mitigated by training on diverse/realistic problem distributions.

strengths: Substantial benchmark scale and realism: The benchmark spans eight diverse CO problems (MIS, MDS, TSP, CVRP, CFLP, CPMP, FJSP, STP) and pushes problem scale up to millions of nodes (e.g., 10M nodes for TSP, 8M for MIS), moving substantially beyond toy synthetic benchmarks that have dominated ML4CO research.

Comprehensive cross-paradigm evaluation: The paper brings together 16 representative ML solvers—encompassing end-to-end neural networks, neural-classical hybrids, and LLM-based agentic code generators—evaluated alongside established domain-specific and commercial exact/heuristic solvers under standardized protocols.

Insightful diagnostic analyses: The ablation studies (e.g., isolating whether neural modules actually help over base heuristics, comparing Euclidean vs. non-Euclidean STP instances, and analyzing algorithm primitives synthesized by LLMs) provide useful takeaways regarding current limitations in representation, inductive biases, and scalability.

Sobering and timely empirical reality check: By evaluating out-of-distribution generalization and large-scale performance, the paper convincingly reveals the gap between classical SOTA and ML approaches, tempering overly optimistic claims often reported on small synthetic benchmarks.
weaknesses: Asymmetry in neural model training vs. testing: Most neural baselines are evaluated using pre-existing checkpoints trained on small synthetic instances (e.g., unit square 2D graphs or fixed-size instances). While evaluating generalization to real-world instances and extreme scale is a legitimate test of real-world deployment, this setup essentially tests zero-shot cross-distribution generalization; it leaves open whether domain-adapted or fine-tuned neural models could narrow the gap.

Limited exploration of underlying LLMs for agentic methods: The LLM agent experiments (FunSearch, Self-Refine, ReEvo) rely exclusively on a single base LLM (o4-mini). Given how heavily agentic code generation and heuristic synthesis depend on model capacity, context length, and base reasoning strength, testing multiple model backbones would provide a clearer picture of LLM solver capabilities.

Handling of OOM and infeasibility in summary metrics: Assigning a maximum primal gap of 1.0 (100%) and 3600s runtime to runs that crashed immediately due to OOM or returned infeasible solutions penalizes failures appropriately, but mixing these failure values into arithmetic means can obscure the actual optimization quality on instances where models did succeed. Reporting success/completion rates alongside conditional gap metrics would offer clearer resolution.
